value: This dissertation employs a three-phase, mixed-methods design. Phase 1 is a critical review (Paré et al., 2015) of AI literacy frameworks and review papers from 2015 to 2025, synthesizing their theoretical and pedagogical implications for early childhood education. Phase 2 uses a techno-ethnographic mixed-methods approach (Pink et al., 2016; Kien, 2008), combining an online survey and home-based inquiry with 8-10 parent-child dyads to capture both the breadth and depth of parents’ perspectives and mediation practices on family technology use. Phase 3 adopts a participatory co-design methodology (DiSalvo et al., 2017), engaging parent–child dyads in iterative, home-based activities that explore adaptable AI literacy themes. In this way, design functions as both a method for generating data and a means of refining practical supports. Data analysis follows an iterative, multi-layered strategy. In Phase 1, framework and thematic synthesis (Booth et al., 2016) map existing frameworks onto the functional, relational, and critical framings and interpret them through the ethics-of-care lens. In Phases 2, survey data are analyzed using descriptive and basic inferential statistics. Qualitative data, including open-ended survey responses, home visit notes, recordings, and interview transcripts, are analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and in vivo coding (Braun & Clarke, 2006). In Phase 3, family-recorded interactions are analyzed through discourse and interactional analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995; Goodwin, 2000), triangulated with weekly reflections, interviews, fieldnotes, family-created artifacts, and researcher memos through artifact and content analysis. Across all three phases, the early AI literacies framework is continuously refined through movement between theory, empirical inquiry, and design. Preliminary findings Phase 1 resulted in an Early AI Literacies Framework as shown in Figure 1. The functional framing, at the core, defines why AI is taught and which concepts, tools, and representations are emphasized. Surrounding this core, relational practices make functional ideas learnable and create space for critical reflection. The critical framing forms the outer layer, connecting to broader sociocultural and ethical contexts. An ethics of care may serve as connective tissue guiding implementation: it grounds the functional in developmental sensitivity, deepens the relational through empathy and reciprocity, and sharpens the critical through moral accountability and justice. Phase 2 and Phase 3 data collection will be conducted from Spring 2026 to Fall 2027, primarily in participants’ homes. Participants will be recruited through a Chinese school, a Girl Scout troop, a public school, and local libraries to capture a wide range of family experiences and perspectives on AI. Figure 1 A Care-Centered Integration of Three Framings in Early AI Literacies Expected contributions This dissertation bridges theory, perception, and practice to reimagine AI literacy as a care-centered, co- constructed process within family ecologies. It aims to contribute: (1) a theoretically grounded early AI literacies framework that provides conceptual and practical guidance for learning and design; (2) empirical insights into how parents conceptualize and negotiate AI in daily life; and (3) evidence of family co-learning through participatory co-design, resulting in practical, low-barrier tools such as the Family AI Literacy Starter Kit.
